artists.biography:
Georgios Kyriacos Panayiotou (25 June 1963 – 25 December 2016), known professionally as George Michael, was an English singer, songwriter, record producer, and philanthropist who rose to fame as a member of the music duo Wham! He was best known for his work in the 1980s and 1990s, including hit singles such as "Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go" and "Last Christmas", and albums such as Faith (1987) and Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1 (1990).

Michael sold more than 100 million records worldwide. His debut solo album, Faith, sold more than 20 million copies worldwide. Michael achieved seven number one singles in the UK and eight number one songs on the Billboard Hot 100 in the US, including "Careless Whisper" and "Praying for Time". He ranks among the best-selling British acts of all time, and in 2008 he was ranked 40th on Billboard's list of the Greatest Hot 100 Artists of All Time. Michael won various music awards throughout his 30-year career, including three Brit Awards—he won Best British Male twice, four MTV Video Music Awards, four Ivor Novello Awards, three American Music Awards, and two Grammy Awards from eight nominations. Michael, who came out as gay in 1998, was an active LGBT rights campaigner and HIV/AIDS charity fundraiser.

In 2004, the Radio Academy named Michael the most played artist on British radio during the period 1984–2004. The documentary A Different Story (released in 2005) covered his career and personal life. Michael's first tour in 15 years, the worldwide 25 Live tour, spanned three tours over the course of three years (2006, 2007, and 2008). In the early hours of 25 December 2016, Michael, aged 53, was found dead in bed at his Oxfordshire home.

apple_music.editorial_notes: 100 Best Albums After proving the depth, scope and maturity of his songwriting with an unassailable debut, George Michael released his second solo album, which feels like a pointed gear change. True, there is “Freedom! ’90”, a bright, piano-driven single designed to deftly skewer both the emerging age of music video culture and Michael’s own conflict about the way the Faith era had almost turned him into a piece of caricatured public property. Nonetheless, the pervading mood of Listen Without Prejudice is one of subtlety, political consciousness and emotional desolation. Woodwinds evoke sparse battlefields (“Mothers Pride”), echo adds ghostly desperation (most notably on the spine-tingling Stevie Wonder cover, “They Won’t Go When I Go”) and windblown acoustic guitar nods to folk (“Something to Save”). Crowned by the grand, Lennon-ian sweep of “Praying for Time”, it is a quietly radical, deeply affecting creative progression—the sound of an artist retreating from pop’s synth-driven orthodoxy into something touched by timelessness, profundity and, in almost every sense, real soul.

lastfm.wiki_content: "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" is the second solo studio album by the English singer-songwriter George Michael, released on 3 September 1990 by Epic Records in the United Kingdom and on 11 September by Columbia Records in the United States. It was Michael's final album of new material on Columbia until "Patience" in 2004. The album differed from Michael's previous album, "Faith" (1987), incorporating largely acoustic instrumentation and a more subdued approach to many of its lyrics and melodies. It topped the UK Albums Chart, while lower sales in the United States contributed to Michael's subsequent legal dispute with Sony Music, during which he argued that the company had not fully supported him as an artist. "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" was reissued in several formats on 20 October 2017 and again reached number one on the UK Albums Chart, 27 years after its original release. After the success of "Faith", expectations for Michael's next album were high. Michael sought to establish himself as a songwriter beyond his previous pop image, resulting in a more restrained and introspective recording. As with "Faith", Michael produced and arranged all of the album's tracks himself. Recording began in July 1989 at producer Chris Porter's house near Guildford before moving to Metropolis Studios in Chiswick, London. According to Tony Parsons, the album was initially planned as a double album containing around 16 original songs written by Michael. By late September 1989, the plan had been abandoned in favour of two separate albums, both scheduled for release in 1990. "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" was released in September 1990. It sold approximately eight million copies worldwide. In the United States, the album entered the Billboard 200 at number 22 and peaked at number two. It remained in the top 10 for the rest of 1990 and spent 42 weeks on the chart. In the United Kingdom, "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" entered the UK Albums Chart at number one. It remained at number two for the following two weeks and spent 34 consecutive weeks in the top 20. In its 24th week, it rose from number 13 to number three. The album spent 88 weeks on the chart and was certified quadruple platinum by the British Phonographic Industry on 2 January 1992. A planned follow-up album, "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 2", was reportedly scheduled for release in June 1991 but was ultimately cancelled. Three tracks intended for the album were released on the 1992 charity compilation "Red Hot + Dance", while "Crazy Man Dance" appeared as the B-side of the compilation's first single, "Too Funky". The first single from "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1", "Praying for Time", was released in August 1990. It reached number six on the UK Singles Chart and number one on the US Billboard Hot 100, becoming Michael's final US number-one single as a solo artist. The second single, and third in the United States, "Waiting for That Day", was released more than a month after the album. The song incorporates a lyric from the Rolling Stones' "You Can't Always Get What You Want", resulting in Mick Jagger and Keith Richards receiving co-writing credits. It reached number 23 in the United Kingdom and number 27 in the United States. In the United States, "Mother's Pride", the B-side of "Waiting for That Day", reached number 46. The song received significant radio airplay in the United States during the Gulf War, partly because of its subject matter. The album's third single, and second in the United States, "Freedom! '90", became one of Michael's best-known songs. It reached number eight in the United States and received a gold certification from the Recording Industry Association of America. In the United Kingdom, it peaked at number 28. The fourth single, "Heal the Pain", reached number 31 on the UK Singles Chart in February 1991. The fifth single, "Cowboys and Angels", entered the chart in March and peaked at number 45. "Soul Free" was released as the sixth and final single in North America, Japan and Australia, where it reached number 95. Michael did not appear in the music videos for the album's singles. The video for "Praying for Time" therefore consisted of the song's lyrics displayed against a dark background. The video for "Freedom! '90", directed by David Fincher, featured several supermodels lip-syncing the lyrics, alongside scenes depicting the destruction of objects associated with Michael's "Faith" period. "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" was reissued on 20 October 2017 as "Listen Without Prejudice / MTV Unplugged". The reissue had first been announced in September 2016. The two-CD edition contains a remastered version of the original album on the first disc and Michael's "MTV Unplugged" concert, recorded at 3 Mills Studios in London on 11 October 1996, on the second. The "MTV Unplugged" disc includes performances of "I Can't Make You Love Me" and "The Strangest Thing" that had previously appeared as B-sides to the single "Older", as well as a 2017 version of "Fantasy" reworked by Nile Rodgers and released as a single in September 2017. The three-CD and DVD deluxe edition includes a CD containing B-sides, remixes and rarities, and a DVD containing a documentary and music videos. The rarities include "If You Were My Woman", recorded live at the Nelson Mandela 70th Birthday Tribute concert in 1988 and included on the "Praying for Time" single, as well as "Crazy Man Dance", "Do You Really Want to Know" and "Happy", the latter three associated with "Red Hot + Dance". The original album was also reissued on vinyl. "Listen Without Prejudice / MTV Unplugged" entered the UK Albums Chart at number one with first-week sales of 56,088 copies, 27 years after the original album had topped the chart. "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" received generally positive reviews from music critics. Mat Snow of Q wrote that the album demonstrated Michael's songwriting ability. Greg Kot of the Chicago Tribune praised its sparse production and described it as evidence that Michael was more than a conventional pop performer. James Hunter of Rolling Stone wrote that the album succeeded in presenting Michael as a serious artist. Chris Willman of the Los Angeles Times praised its melodies, production and personal subject matter. Stuart Maconie of NME considered the album short of hooks and a sense of lightness but viewed it as part of Michael's artistic development. Some critics were less positive. Greg Sandow of Entertainment Weekly considered the album less lively and enjoyable than "Faith" and argued that its subject matter was insufficiently challenging. Robert Christgau of The Village Voice characterised the album as "cocktail music" and was unconvinced by Michael's reflections on fame. "Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1" won the award for Best British Album at the 1991 Brit Awards. The album was included in the book "1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die". Apple Music included it at number 91 on its "100 Best Albums" list. In 2003, Sal Cinquemani of Slant Magazine described the album as a personal statement and argued that its subdued character contributed to its reception among listeners accustomed to Michael's earlier material. Slant Magazine also included it on its 2003 list of 50 Essential Pop Albums. AllMusic reviewer Stephen Thomas Erlewine criticised some aspects of the album, including Michael's reduced emphasis on melodic hooks and the directness of some of its socially conscious lyrics, while considering several of its songs representative of his abilities as a pop songwriter. Reviewing the 2017 reissue for Pitchfork, Alfred Soto discussed the album in the context of the HIV/AIDS epidemic and the musical climate of the early 1990s. Soto compared its subdued character with "Behaviour", the 1990 album by the Pet Shop Boys, and interpreted the prevalence of ballads and elegiac material among some artists of the period in relation to the social circumstances surrounding the epidemic. He also argued that the album's original form represented a continuation of the artistic direction established by "Faith", while viewing the 2017 edition as a broader collection reflecting different aspects of Michael's work. perplexity.description:
Released in 1990 on Epic Records, Listen Without Prejudice Vol. 1 marked a decisive move away from the polished dance-pop image of George Michael’s Faith. Across its ten tracks, Michael combines sophisticated pop songwriting with electronic textures, funk and soul influences, acoustic intimacy, gospel feeling, and understated orchestration. “Praying for Time” and “Freedom! ’90” balance social unease with irresistible hooks, while “Cowboys and Angels,” “Mother’s Pride,” and “They Won’t Go When We Go” reveal a more reflective, emotionally exposed performer.

Initially viewed as a commercial disappointment beside Faith, the album has since become widely regarded as a modern pop classic. It sold more than eight million copies worldwide, won the 1991 Brit Award for Best British Album, and ultimately established Michael as an artist with greater creative ambition than his early pop-star image suggested. The 2017 remastered reissue expanded the original album with previously unreleased material and MTV Unplugged, reinforcing its lasting significance—an especially fitting choice for National Album Day 2026.
